newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban Afghan offensive against Masood stalls.
newsitem.headline: Taleban Afghan offensive against Masood stalls.

text.p: A Taleban offensive against the valley stronghold of Afghanistan's former government army chief Ahmad Shah Masood appeared to have stalled on Monday as the two sides exchanged sporadic mortar and artillery fire.
Bearded Taleban warriors said they had been shipped in as reinforcements for a new assault on mountains surrounding the Panjsher valley, the heavily fortified redoubt of Masood.

Bulldozers entered the valley north of Kabul to clear mines and landslides detonated ahead of Masood's retreat, with the Taleban making limited progress along the valley floor after their offensive began on Saturday.

"The main objective now is to take that mountain where the shooting is coming from," said one fighter, pointing to a peak several kilometres (miles) away sprouting occasional plumes of smoke and dust from Taleban tank shells.
It was not clear how much ground the Taleban, seeking to crush one of two remaining armies not allied to it or under its control, had made through military means since the offensive started.

Some locals rejected Taleban claims that it had taken by force the two hills at the entrance to the steep-sided valley, saying locally born Masood had withdrawn for fear of shelling of civilians or the town of Golbahar at the mouth of the gorge.
In the town, which straddles the rocky Panjsher river, streets nearest the valley were largely deserted, with only a few shops open.
Old men and women and children wandered the dusty mainstreet, sidestepping mounds of shell casings and jeeps loaded with Taleban fighters that revved past.
Military analysts have questioned whether the Taleban are capable of taking the 150-km (95-mile) long valley, which Masood successfully defended against Soviet firepower in the 1980s.

The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) earlier quoted a statement issued by warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who holds areas west of the Panjsher, that he would "defend any compatriot" attacked by the Taleban, apparently threatening the Islamic militia with retaliation if they kept attacking Masood.
The Taleban came under fire on Sunday as rockets and mortars rained on forces gathering for a second major assault on mountains overlooking the valley, sending turbaned fighters running for cover.
Monday was quieter, although mortar rounds fired from mountain-tops were still landing on positions occupied by Taleban tanks and anti-aircraft guns.
"We are just waiting for orders," said one Taleban fighter. Another said the offensive would restart on Monday night. "The elders are still talking," he said.

This latest offensive has been the first serious warfare since the Taleban took over the capital Kabul on September 27. The capital fell with little resistance from forces of President Burhanuddin Rabbani.
The Taleban have in two years emerged from obscurity as religious students on the Pakistan border in the south to capture three-quarters of the country.

Some people in Kabul have welcomed their victory as an end to years of factional warfare but others have been critical of their strict brand of Islam which limits the role of women and demands men pray five times a day.
Only Masood, Rabbani's top commander until the two were ousted from power ten days ago, and warlord Dostum control areas outside the Taleban's grip, both of them in the north of the country.
But commanders of the purist Islamic army said they were confident of victory.
